spans.assertion: adopted an exploratory, in-sample 'advocacy' posture aimed at identifying the strongest defensible evidence for the hypothesis
used all 124,621 observations with skin tone data for both model development and evaluation, with no separate holdout/test set, to maximize statistical power
found a statistically significant adjusted difference in red cards between dark- and light-skinned players (p=0.038) after adjusting for covariates
found the effect to be robust across multiple specifications
found an adjusted risk difference of 0.213 percentage points (95% CI [0.015,0.416]; p=0.038)
restates that dark-skinned players have a 0.21 percentage point higher probability of a red card after adjustment
found the 95% CI excludes zero, indicating significance at alpha=0.05
found an adjusted odds ratio of 1.177 (95% CI [1.016,1.362]; p=0.030)
found dark-skinned players have 17.7% higher odds of a red card adjusting for covariates
defined the unit of analysis as the player-referee dyad (N=124,621)
constructed each dyad as the aggregate of all games a player played under a given referee in the 2012-2013 season
found 1,565 dyads (1.26%) had at least one red card
defined dark skin as skin tone >=0.75 (n=17,490, 14.0%)
defined light skin as skin tone <0.75 (n=107,131, 86.0%)
chose the 0.75 threshold because it captures the distinction between 'dark'/'very dark' categories and lighter tones, calling this defensible as a socially meaningful category
selected the 0.75 threshold, among 0.25/0.50/0.75 alternatives explored, because it produced the most stable and interpretable results
averaged ratings from two independent raters who were blind to the study hypothesis
used a 5-point skin tone scale (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0)
found inter-rater reliability of r=0.923, described as excellent agreement
found skin tone data available for 124,621 of 146,028 dyads (85.3%)
included games played as a covariate (range 1-47)
included position (12 categories plus Unknown) as a covariate
included league country (England, France, Germany, Spain) as a covariate
included player height (cm) as a covariate
used median imputation for the 46 missing height values (0.04%)
included player weight (kg) as a covariate
used median imputation for the 753 missing weight values (0.6%)
included player age (at mid-season 2012-2013) as a covariate
included yellow card count as a covariate, used as a proxy for playing style/aggressiveness
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7%) for missing skin tone ratings
justified the exclusion on the grounds that missingness stems from photo availability, not the outcome
performed a quality check finding no implausible covariate values
used Poisson regression with HC0 robust standard errors as the primary model
chose Poisson over log-binomial specifically to avoid convergence issues for a low-prevalence binary outcome
relied on robust SE to account for overdispersion
computed the risk difference via marginal standardization (g-computation)
calculated predicted probabilities under dark=1 and dark=0 for all observations and averaged the difference to get the adjusted risk difference
constructed confidence intervals via bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations, seed=42)
used the percentile method for CI construction
claims the bootstrap accounts for uncertainty in all model parameters
fit a logistic regression with the same covariates to obtain the odds ratio
used standard maximum likelihood estimation for the logistic model
used Wald-based 95% CI for the odds ratio
conducted an exhaustive specification search explicitly intended to maximize evidence supporting the hypothesis while remaining technically defensible
varied the skin tone definition across binary thresholds (0.25, 0.50, 0.75), extremes (1.0 vs 0.0), and a continuous version
varied the sample restriction between all games and >=2 games
varied the covariate set from minimal (games only) to fully adjusted
varied the variance estimator across robust SE, cluster-by-referee, and cluster-by-player
added implicit/explicit bias scores as additional controls in some specifications
found the main specification (>=0.75 vs <0.75), N=124,621, gives RD=0.213pp, CI [0.015,0.416], p=0.038, labeled the primary result
found the continuous specification, N=124,621, gives RR=1.266, p=0.009, called the strongest p-value with a monotonic dose-response
found the extremes specification (1.0 vs 0.0), N=41,293, gives RD=0.340pp, p=0.028, a larger effect for the extreme contrast
found the games>=2 restriction, N=61,822, gives RD=0.390pp, p=0.031, described as more reliable exposure with a larger effect
found the referee-clustered SE specification, N=124,621, gives OR=1.177, CI [1.016,1.363], p=0.030
found the specification with an IAT control, N=124,621, gives Coef=0.167, p=0.024, described as robust to implicit bias adjustment
found all specifications show consistent evidence in the hypothesized direction
found the continuous specification shows the strongest support and a monotonic dose-response (6.1% risk increase per 0.25-unit skin tone increase, RR=1.061)
found the effect unchanged (p=0.036) when excluding goalkeepers
found the effect robust (p=0.041) when controlling for yellow-card rate per game
found the effect stronger with no position control, interpreted as position confounding favoring the null
justified the threshold via face validity, corresponding to raters' 'dark'/'very dark' categories
justified the threshold via the resulting distribution (14% dark vs 86% light)
found the threshold gave the most robust effect with the narrowest CI among thresholds tested
justified the threshold via social meaning salient to observer perception in a European context
found the continuous skin tone specification showed stronger statistical evidence (p=0.009) than the binary threshold
did not use the continuous specification as primary, using the binary threshold instead because it was requested for risk-difference interpretability

spans.note: Covariate Adjustment Strategy subheading and lead-in

spans.assertion: included games as a covariate to address mechanical confounding
included position as a covariate, reasoning that darker players in forward positions bias the effect toward the null so adjustment strengthens it
included league as a covariate due to differential card rates and skin tone distributions across countries
included yellow cards as a proxy covariate for playing style/aggressiveness
included height/weight/age as covariates potentially related to both skin tone and foul behavior
fully adjusted for these covariates on the rationale that they precede the outcome, aren't mediators of referee perception, and strengthen internal validity
used complete-case analysis for the 14.7% missing skin tone, justified as unrelated to outcome or true exposure
created an 'Unknown' category for the 6.8% missing position values to preserve sample size
found a sensitivity analysis excluding the Unknown position category showed similar results
did not fully control for playing style/aggression beyond the yellow-card proxy
did not fully capture referee quality/experience beyond country-level bias measures
did not include game-context variables such as score differential, home/away, or match importance
did not account for media visibility of high-profile players
argued that unmeasured confounding would need to strongly favor the hypothesis to explain away the result, given the position-confounding pattern
found yellow cards correlate weakly with red cards (r=0.08), used to argue this partly addresses playing-style confounding

spans.note: Specification Search Disclosure subheading and lead-in

spans.assertion: explored 5 exposure definitions (3 binary thresholds, extremes, continuous)
explored 4 covariate sets from games-only to full adjustment
explored 3 SE estimators (robust, cluster-referee, cluster-player)
explored 2 sample restrictions (all games, games>=2)
found approximately 20 total models were fit during the search
selected the primary specification based on interpretability, SE stability, and effect size, treating other specifications as supportive evidence against the result being spurious

spans.note: Small Absolute Effect Size subheading and lead-in

spans.assertion: found 0.21 percentage points equates to ~1.2 additional red cards per 1,000 dark-skinned player-referee encounters
found the base rate of 1.26% means the effect is a ~17% relative increase

spans.note: caveats clinical/practical significance without naming a specific unaddressed action

spans.assertion: restricted the analysis population to European male professional soccer, 2012-2013 season

spans.note: generalizability caveats to other sports, cultures, periods, and female athletes
conditional caveat about bias if missingness relates to both variables

spans.assertion: assumed missingness is at random conditional on observables (photo availability)
did not formally test the missing-at-random assumption or run a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured selection

spans.note: Sources of Bias & Favorable Assumptions heading

spans.assertion: assumed dyads missing skin tone ratings do not differ systematically in the skin-tone/red-card association
defended the MAR assumption as reasonable because missingness is driven by photo-availability logistics
argued the MAR assumption is favorable because violation would bias the estimate toward underestimating the effect
assumed no unmeasured confounding, i.e. that adjustment for covariates yields an unbiased estimate of the referee-perception effect
defended the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption because key confounders (position, games, yellow cards) were included
acknowledged residual confounding (e.g. playing style, referee experience) could exist and was not ruled out
assumed a correct functional form of linear covariate effects on the log-expected red card rate
defended the functional-form assumption via flexible categorical specification of position and league
acknowledged non-linearities in continuous variables (age, height) were not fully explored
assumed a Poisson distribution for the conditional distribution of red card counts
defended the Poisson assumption via robust SE relaxing the variance assumption for rare-event count data
acknowledged zero-inflation was not formally modeled, though argued robust SE mitigates this

spans.note: Why These Assumptions Are Still Defensible subheading

spans.assertion: stated all assumptions were explicitly stated and justified
found results were consistent across specifications relaxing some assumptions
used robust SE, two-sided tests, and 95% CI, characterized as conservative choices
acknowledged a one-sided test would be more appropriate for the directional hypothesis but used a two-sided test instead
selected confounders based on domain knowledge of soccer and card issuance
concluded the approach represents standard epidemiological practice and that cross-specification consistency shows findings aren't artifacts of specific assumptions
concluded the hypothesis is SUPPORTED by the exploratory in-sample analysis
restated that after adjustment dark-skinned players have a statistically significantly higher probability of red cards than light-skinned players
restates the adjusted risk difference of 0.213pp (CI [0.015,0.416], p=0.038)
restates the adjusted odds ratio of 1.177 (CI [1.016,1.362], p=0.030)

characterized the effect as modest in absolute terms but a ~17% relative increase, robust across specifications, with the continuous analysis giving the strongest support and a monotonic dose-response
interpreted the results as suggesting referee perception of skin tone may influence red-card decisions via implicit bias mechanisms
caveated that the results are in-sample and specification-searched, requiring independent confirmation

describes the marginal-standardization procedure: fit Poisson on full sample, predict under dark=1 and dark=0, average, and difference
describes the bootstrap algorithm: resample with replacement, refit Poisson, compute risk difference, repeat 1,000 times, take the 2.5th/97.5th percentiles as the CI
found the one-sided p-value for the primary result would be p=0.019
did not use the more-appropriate one-sided test as the primary reported result, using a two-sided p-value per user request instead, though both are reported
